note_tweet.text:
A recent post on X, captioned simply "uni student life", has accumulated over 140 million views. It contains no argument and no information; it consists only of photographs of a young woman holding coffee in a lecture theatre, leaning back in a sunlit café, and working at a laptop with a textbook splayed open beside her. That such a slight artefact should command an audience larger than the population of most nations is itself worth examining, and the ensuing comment thread, in which one user observes that everybody in the replies is miserable while her own impoverished university years were wonderful, exposes the fault line running beneath the entire genre.

The first point to make is that the post is not a record of student life but a composition about it. Every element has been selected for legibility: the paper cup, the pristine notebook, the oblique angle that catches the light falling through an institutional window. What is conspicuously absent is everything that constitutes the actual substance of study, namely the confusion, the repetition, the hours that yield nothing, the seminar in which one understands very little and says even less. The genre performs intellectual labour without depicting it, much as a photograph of running shoes performs fitness. Consequently, viewers are invited to desire not education itself but the visual signature of having received one, and this substitution is precisely what makes the imagery so frictionless and so widely consumable.

A second and more consequential effect is the distortion of comparison. Social media does not present us with a representative sample of our peers; it presents us with an aggregate of their most flattering moments, assembled into a composite person who does not exist. A student who has spent an afternoon failing to understand a proof will encounter this composite and conclude, not unreasonably, that her own experience is aberrant. The resulting demoralisation is often misdiagnosed as a personal deficiency when it is in fact a statistical artefact, an inevitable consequence of measuring an unedited interior against a curated exterior. Anxiety of this kind is corrosive in a specific way: it redirects energy away from the work and towards the anxious monitoring of how one's work appears.

Yet the reply quoted above complicates any straightforwardly critical reading, and it deserves to be taken seriously rather than dismissed as contrarianism. The commenter's insistence that she was penniless and nonetheless flourished suggests that the aesthetic and the experience are separable, and that pleasure in learning does not in fact depend on the accoutrements the genre fetishises. At the same time, her remark that she could see the Eiffel Tower from her classroom quietly reintroduces the very privilege she means to disclaim. This is instructive. Attending a Parisian institution is not a neutral baseline from which to reassure others, and the episode illustrates how easily discussions of authenticity are conducted from positions that are themselves highly particular. The disagreement in that thread is therefore not merely about attitude; it is about unevenly distributed circumstances that no amount of reframing can dissolve.

It would nevertheless be excessively severe to condemn the genre outright. Photographing one's desk is a mild and largely harmless pleasure, and there is something genuinely sustaining in making an ordinary Tuesday appear worthy of attention. Students who find that ritual motivating are not deceiving themselves so much as practising a small, benign form of self-encouragement. The difficulty arises only when the representation begins to govern the activity, when a person studies in a particular café because it photographs well, or feels that an afternoon of unglamorous, unwitnessed effort somehow did not count.

The reasonable conclusion, then, is neither wholesale rejection nor uncritical participation, but a deliberate reordering of priorities. The value of a university education resides in capacities that are structurally invisible to a camera: the gradual acquisition of a difficult method, the willingness to remain with a problem that resists, the slow formation of judgement. None of these photograph well, and none of them will ever accumulate 140 million views. That is not a defect in them. It is simply a reminder that the most important things a student does are, by their nature, unpostable, and that a life spent optimising for the visible will reliably impoverish the part that actually matters.
